title: Decision trees: classification with questions
intro: A decision tree sorts data with yes/no questions — no formulas, no coefficients. The most explainable model in scikit-learn, and at the same time the textbook example of overfitting.
keyPoints: A tree splits the data with yes/no questions (feature + threshold) until its leaves are pure: each leaf predicts one class.
Each split picks the feature + threshold that reduces impurity the most — measured with Gini or entropy.
Trees need no scaling and capture non-linear patterns — but without a brake they grow themselves into overfitting.
Brakes: max_depth, min_samples_split and min_samples_leaf — see the topic Bias-variance tradeoff.

blocks.html: Every internal node asks one question of the form “is feature \( x_j \) below threshold \( t \)?”; the leaves give the final verdict: the majority class in that leaf.
Loan example: “income €2500 or higher?” → yes → “debt < €500?” → yes → leaf approved. A new application falls through the tree top to bottom — a path you can literally explain to a customer.
The decision boundary is a composition of straight lines (axis-parallel splits): non-linear as a whole, built from simple pieces.

sections.title: Splitting: where do you cut the data?

blocks.html: The split: pick one feature and one threshold, divide the samples into two groups. scikit-learn tries every (feature, threshold) combination and keeps the split that separates the groups most cleanly.
The search is greedy and top-down (CART): start at the root, pick the best split now, repeat on both halves. The tree never looks ahead and never revisits earlier choices.
Demo: eight samples, two features; the root mixes 3 approved (✓) and 5 rejected (✗) applications.
One split rarely suffices: every impure child gets its own new split, until each leaf is pure or a stopping condition (depth, minimum samples) kicks in.
With positive fraction \( p \) in a node there are two standard impurity measures — both 0 for a pure node and maximal at 50/50:

blocks.label: Gini impurity
blocks.caption: The probability that two random samples from the node have different classes. Max 0.5 at p = 0.5 — the scikit-learn default.

blocks.label: Entropy
blocks.caption: The ‘chaos’ in bits; max 1 at p = 0.5. Virtually identical in shape to Gini — in practice the choice hardly matters.

blocks.title: Gini and entropy as a function of p
blocks.subtitle: Drag the slider: at p = 0 or 1 the node is pure (both measures 0), at p = 0.5 the mixture is maximal. The live metrics follow along.

blocks.html: The tree picks the split that minimizes the weighted average impurity of the children (highest information gain). “Weighted” is essential: a small dirty child counts less than a large one.
Worked out for “income ≤ 2500”: root \( G = 0.469 \); children \( \tfrac{6}{8} \cdot 0.278 + \tfrac{2}{8} \cdot 0 = 0.208 \) — a solid drop.
In scikit-learn you pick the measure with criterion: "gini" (default) or "entropy". In practice both yield nearly identical trees.

sections.title: When does the tree stop? The overfit trap

blocks.html: A tree that grows until every leaf is pure always reaches 100% training accuracy — because eventually each leaf holds exactly one sample. That is not learning but memorizing the training data.

rows: the number of questions below the root
a node with fewer samples will not split
every leaf keeps at least n samples
prediction is a majority over enough data
a hard cap on model size

blocks.html: The brakes shift the balance between bias (too flat) and variance (too deep) — for trees max_depth is the textbook knob.
The standard three: fit, predict, score — no scaler needed, thresholds are scale-independent. The example trains one unrestricted and one restricted tree on the breast cancer dataset:

blocks.caption: unrestricted vs. pruned tree on breast_cancer
blocks.source:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)

# 1) tree without a brake: grows until every leaf is pure
tree_free = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42)
tree_free.fit(X_tr, y_tr)

# 2) tree with a brake: at most 3 questions deep
tree_pruned = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=42)
tree_pruned.fit(X_tr, y_tr)

print('unrestricted: train', round(tree_free.score(X_tr, y_tr), 3),
      '| test', round(tree_free.score(X_te, y_te), 3))
print('max_depth=3 : train', round(tree_pruned.score(X_tr, y_tr), 3),
      '| test', round(tree_pruned.score(X_te, y_te), 3))
print('leaves:', tree_free.get_n_leaves(), 'vs',
      tree_pruned.get_n_leaves())

blocks.html: Typical picture: the unrestricted tree sits at 100% train accuracy and loses almost five points on test; the restricted tree tests better (0.958 vs 0.951) with half the leaves.

blocks.caption: reading the tree as human rules
blocks.source:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text

data = load_breast_cancer()
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=0).fit(
    data.data, data.target)

# the first two questions of the tree, with the class per leaf
print(export_text(tree, feature_names=data.feature_names,
                  max_depth=2))

blocks.html: export_text shows the tree as rules — the form you can hand to a domain expert. No other model in scikit-learn is this transparent.
